questions

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.1] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q1
Responses were split between A, B, and C, demonstrating that candidates did not have a clear
understanding of molecular-level processes involved with changes of state.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.2] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q2
The correct response, D, was answered correctly by just over 50% of the candidates. As all responses
were alkenes, the question tested the relationship between empirical and molecular formulas.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.3] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q3
56% of responses were correct, identifying this question as a limiting reactant using gas volumes.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.4] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q4
Half of the candidates correctly identified the smallest downward arrow as the spectrum's red line. One-
quarter of responses chose D the transition ending on level one.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.5] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q5
Most candidates correctly identified the relationships between electronic configuration and period table
position.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.6] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q6
Average performance on a reasonable discriminator question identifying an actinoid.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.7] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q7
Candidates performed well in recognizing the periodic trend in the acidity of the oxides.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.8] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q8
There was good performance on the question that required candidates to work out the oxidization state
of cobalt in a complex ion with chloride and ammonia ligands.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.9] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q9
There was a reasonably good performance on this question relating to the type of bonding and the
properties. Teacher criticism identified response D, "giant molecular", as a weak choice, suggesting that
"giant covalent" is the preferred terminology.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.10] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q10
61.6% of candidates were able to discern the species containing resonance structures.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.11] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q11
Just over half of the candidates could connect the concepts of electron domains, geometry and bond
angle.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.12] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q12
This question asked students to be able to determine the geometry of an extended octet species given
the molecular formula. While 42% of the responses were correct, the second most popular answer was the
distractor with no lone pairs, indicating that students perhaps didn't recognize the difference between
electron domain and molecular geometry.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.13] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q13
Candidates demonstrated average performance in identifying ozone-depleting gases.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.14] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q14
Candidates performed reasonably well in being able to substitute values correctly in the calorimetric
calculations.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.15] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q15
There was a weak performance in this question, asking candidates to match the arithmetic and data
sources for determining the heat of reaction from different standard heats.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.16] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q16
Over 65% of students could recognize an equation representing electron affinity in this discriminating
question.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.17] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q17
This discriminating question was well done. Candidates were able to identify decreased entropy in a
chemical equation.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.18] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q18
This question on the practical aspects of tracking the reaction rate was well done and a good discriminator.

Over two-thirds of candidates could correctly identify the effect of concentration changes on the rate

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.20] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q20
This was the second most well-answered question, with just over 80% of candidates being able to process
rate data to determine the overall order of reaction.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.21] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q21
There was good performance in interpreting the components of the Arrhenius equation.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.22] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q22
There was a reasonable performance on the relationship between equilibrium constants.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.23] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q23
This question testing the relationship between equilibrium constants, position and free energy was the
strongest discriminator and had a 58% success rate.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.24] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q24
This question identifying conjugate pairs was the most correctly answered, with over 81% correct.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.25] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q25
Only 44% of candidates were able to identify how to distinguish between equimolar solutions of strong
and weak acids

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.26] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q26
53% of candidates correctly identified the relationship between acid strength, pK a and pH.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.27] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q27
There was a good performance in identifying components of a buffer solution.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.28] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q28
Two-thirds of the candidates could determine the oxidation state of bromine in various species.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.29] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q29
Three-quarters of the candidates were able to identify relationships in a voltaic cell.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.30] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q30
There was a weak performance in this electrolysis product question. The correct response, C and the next
most popular answer, A, indicate that candidates could relate "dilute" to the production of oxygen gas at
the anode. However, they could not identify hydrogen as the preferred product over magnesium. This
question drew criticism from teachers, who stated it was unfair without a reactivity series to reference.

This question was a particularly poor discriminator. 45% correctly identified the combination that

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.32] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q32
Good performance on this question identifying a homologous series.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.33] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q33
Candidates were able to identify the name of branched chloroalkane correctly.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.34] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q34

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.35] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q35
There was a level distribution identifying the factors affecting the rate of an SN1 reaction. While the correct
answer was most popular, candidates had trouble interpreting the effect of the leaving group and the
degree of branching.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.36] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q36
Low performance on the rationale for using polar protic solvents in SN1 reactions.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.37] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q37
Candidates performed reasonably in identifying E/Z relationships in alkenes with various halogen
substituents.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.38] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q38
There was a strong performance in calculating the density of a sample to the correct number of significant
figures.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.39] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q39
Approximately 30% of candidates were able to identify the region of the e-m spectrum that is used in 1H
NMR spectroscopy

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.HL.TZ1.40] May 2024 Paper 1 HL Q40
Finally, there was a good performance in stating the significance of the splitting pattern in high-resolution

• Factors affecting rates and mechanisms of organic reaction (e.g. SN1),
• Manipulation of energetics data from various sources,
• VSEPR theory; the explanation of geometry and angles; differentiation between electron domain
geometry and molecular geometry,

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · general] May 2024 Paper 1 SL
A total of 7173 candidates sat the exam in English and the 69 schools that filled in evaluations found the
difficulty of the examination appropriate (92%), and the quality of the paper good.
As can be seen from the table below all questions discriminated quite well. No concerns were raised this
session about the questions or the distractors.
Worryingly, some students are still leaving answers blank although there is no penalty for incorrect
answers.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.SL.TZ1.1] May 2024 Paper 1 SL Q1
Many candidates believed that individual atoms retain their individual properties in a compound.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.SL.TZ1.2] May 2024 Paper 1 SL Q2
Many candidates incorrectly believed the highest peak of 42 determined the molar mass instead of the
peak of highest mass at 70.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.SL.TZ1.4] May 2024 Paper 1 SL Q4
Many candidates struggled to identify the limiting reagent and hence the gasses left after the reaction
had finished.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.SL.TZ1.6] May 2024 Paper 1 SL Q6
The identification of the change leading to the red line in the emission spectrum of hydrogen proved
challenging.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.SL.TZ1.12] May 2024 Paper 1 SL Q12
Most candidates recognised that the molecule was bent but many chose the incorrect bond angle of 105
instead of 117.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.SL.TZ1.15] May 2024 Paper 1 SL Q15
Proved very challenging as it required a good understanding of all of the different energy changes studied
in topic 5 and how to do calculations with them.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.SL.TZ1.23] May 2024 Paper 1 SL Q23
Was very poorly done and the majority of students incorrectly stated that the ions would be formed at the
electrodes rather than the elements.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.SL.TZ1.26] May 2024 Paper 1 SL Q26
Required students to know what happens when a secondary alcohol is oxidized. Even though it was a very
straightforward question it was very poorly answered.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.SL.TZ1.27] May 2024 Paper 1 SL Q27
Was also problematic as candidates thought that hydrogen would be a product of incomplete
combustion.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.1.SL.TZ1.30] May 2024 Paper 1 SL Q30
Unfortunately very few candidates were aware that H-NMR uses radio waves

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · recommendations] May 2024 Paper 1 SL
Students must read multiple choice questions very carefully and eliminate incorrect answers, so they can
identify the best answer to the question.
a        International Baccalaureate
Baccalaureat International
Bachillerato Internacional
Students should use a highlighter on the examination paper to ensure they do not miss any important
information.
It is important to practice doing calculations without the use of a calculator.
Students should draw Lewis structures for a variety of species, as well as identifying their geometry and
determining the bond and molecular polarity.
Ensure that all parts of the syllabus including the Organic Chemistry and Spectroscopy sections of the
syllabus are taught fully.
Finally, no answers should be left blank as there is not any negative marking, but there is a 25% chance of
a correct answer by guessing.

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · general] May 2024 Paper 2 HL
Sixty-two schools completed the G2 forms. Almost 90% of teachers who responded to the G2 survey
reported that the exam was “appropriate” in terms of the difficulty, with 9% stating it was “too difficult
”. Over 50% reported that the exam was of similar difficulty to the previous year, with 24% stating it was
a little more difficult. The quality of the paper was “acceptable ” or better in terms of inclusivity,
suitability, readability and presentation. 8% reported that the clarity was less than acceptable.
Some responses expressed surprise at the hydrogen electrode and cell notation as this was not a focus on
previous exams but recognised that it was clearly on the syllabus.
There was some criticism of the wording and anticipated expected responses; for example, the bonding
in sodium citrate can include ionic, covalent and intermolecular forces.
Examiners reported a generally lower quality of responses regarding clarity of arithmetic processing and
precision of language.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.2.HL.TZ1.1] May 2024 Paper 2 HL Q1
Quantitative chemistry responses represented a variety of abilities. Candidates often had weak arithmetic
or rounded answers too much. Many candidates did not clearly understand the difference between
percentage yield and percentage error.
a        International Baccalaureate
Baccalaureat International
Bachillerato Internacional
Many candidates found dealing with citric acid challenging. There was a poor understanding of the
definition of conjugate pairs, and many candidates thought that the alcoholic proton was also acidic.
Explanations relating to the characteristics of weak acids and their conjugates confused the number of
acidic protons with the strength of the acid. Weaker candidates wrongly identified the OH component of
the carboxylic acid as a source of hydroxide ions to justify the alkaline nature of the conjugate base.
Explanations of ionic bonding and the effect of different ions on the hydration and lattice enthalpies
generally lacked precision and understanding of the impact of ionic radius and charge density.
Candidates were able to make a straightforward pH calculation.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.2.HL.TZ1.2] May 2024 Paper 2 HL Q2
The energetics component of the question was generally well done. Most students could determine the
enthalpy of combustion but had a poor understanding of the practical aspects of the question.
lacked precision for example, “use an insulated container” and “
material is necessary to transfer heat into the water.
Comparing the ethanol and propan-1-ol gels proved to be a discriminating question. Stronger candidates
explicitly calculated the energy contained in 1.0 g of substance, while weaker ones only referenced the
data book values insufficient to score points.
Generally, candidates were well-versed in the class and functional group names; however, some did not
understand the difference or answered with formulas.
Candidates were able to identify intermolecular forces.
The 3-D representations of organic compounds and mechanisms and products of their reactions were
poorly done; however, most candidates could identify the esterification reaction and water by-product
but did not know the reaction conditions.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.2.HL.TZ1.3] May 2024 Paper 2 HL Q3
The equilibrium expression and effect of temperature were generally well done, with candidates linking
the enthalpy and the shift to products.
Many candidates struggled with correctly labelling and annotating graphs. For example, many candidates
did not identify the relative temperature curves or confused the curves with the activation energy lines.
Nickel was often identified as a catalyst but lacked correct reasoning. Stronger candidates identified that,
as a solid, nickel                                , therefore, would not appear in the rate expression.
Again, stronger candidates could clearly articulate that the initial mechanistic step determined the rate
law and would not confirm the following steps.
There were a significant number of candidates who could not correctly draw the graph for the rate law
relationship.
RTlnK. Many candidates did not notice that there were two components to question 3g.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.2.HL.TZ1.4] May 2024 Paper 2 HL Q4
Most candidates identified the oxidation states and roles in redox reactions.
A surprising number of candidates drew carbon dioxide as a bent molecule despite no central lone pair.
Many candidates thought carbon dioxide had sp 2 hybridisation and could not correctly identify the
number of sigma and pi bonds.
Solving for the bond enthalpy of the carbon-oxygen triple bond was challenging. Many candidates either
failed to recognise that carbon monoxide had a triple bond and stated the value of the double bond found
in the data book or used the value for the double bond and solved for the total enthalpy.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.2.HL.TZ1.5] May 2024 Paper 2 HL Q5
Candidates performed well in identifying the jump in ionisation energy but sometimes misinterpreted the
data and how it related to the group number.
Many candidates knew that a lower formal charge indicated the preferred Lewis structure. Still, many tried
to assign an overall formal charge instead of identifying the formal charge on each atom in the molecule.
Many candidates did not assign formal charges to each atom in the two structures.
Candidates could identify an appropriate indicator for the titration curve but did not correctly or neatly
adjust the curve for a strong base. Many did not recognise that the endpoint would be the same but
instead shifted the curve to require less sodium hydroxide, presumably confusing strength and
concentration.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.2.HL.TZ1.6] May 2024 Paper 2 HL Q6
Most candidates could determine the relative atomic mass of nickel, but weaker candidates sometimes
rounded the answer to remove the decimal places.
Many candidates failed to identify the atomic number of nickel correctly and then did not recognise it as
a 2+ ion; the consequence was the incorrect orbital diagram.
Explanations of the colour phenomena associated with complex ions challenge candidates. Ligand
strength, the degree of splitting, energy absorption, and the observation of remaining wavelengths were
often confused ideas.
Lewis and Brønsted-Lowry s definitions of acids and bases challenged some candidates. Many candidates
could not write familiar chemical equations with correct formulas, including ionic charges.

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · recommendations] May 2024 Paper 2 HL
Arithmetic procedures candidates should practice solving for different values in enthalpy calculations.
Teachers should hold candidates to a high standard for accurate rounding and significant figures.
Teachers should provide opportunities for candidates to practice stating and explaining the characteristics
of unfamiliar weak acids and bases and their conjugates, definitions of acids and bases, representative
equations, and their structures.
Candidates should practice explaining chemical phenomena in unfamiliar situations and avoid learning
rote explanations that may not answer the question. For example, complex ions, equilibria, bonding, and
kinetics often require explanations of unfamiliar situations
Candidates must be able to provide explanations of chemical bonding, including the effect of size and
charge on attractive forces and clearly identify the species involved.
Teachers should provide opportunities to practice drawing 3-D representations of molecules and
mechanisms in organic chemistry.
Candidates need practice connecting kinetic concepts like Maxwell-Boltzmann diagrams, rate laws and
their associated graphs. When sketching graphs, candidates should clearly identify key aspects of the
graph (e.g. linear vs. proportional)
Candidates should be aware that mathematical manipulations involving quantities with different unit
dimensions must                                              RTlnK.
Students should be more familiar with the rate law graphs and how they agree with the rate law.
Candidates should be encouraged to draw proportional graphs with a ruler and intercept at the origin.
Candidates should have opportunities to practice electronic configurations of various atoms and ions and
their associated magnetic properties.
Candidates should practice drawing electrochemical systems and their representations.

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · general] May 2024 Paper 2 SL

feedback forms received, 92% of respondents stated that the level of difficulty was appropriate and 99%
stated that it was a suitable paper. 82% considered it to be of a similar standard or easier than the
examination in 2023. Despite the accessibility of the paper there still appeared to be significant difficulties
for some students and there were many candidates who did not attempt to answer the questions or
offered responses that were very poor.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.2.SL.TZ1.1] May 2024 Paper 2 SL Q1
(a)(i) There were many excellent answers however there were also some common problems:
• Candidates did not calculate the moles of reactants correctly
• Candidates used masses totalling 100g and not 1g to calculate moles
• Identification of the limiting reagent
(a)(ii) Many candidates could gain an ECF mark for M1 if they applied the correct ratio.
Many candidates used the molar volume at STP of 22.7 which meant M2 was lost
(a)(iii) Calculation of % yield was generally not a problem, as they had 0.068 supplied to them if they did
not did not have an answer. However many tried to calculate % error.
(b)(i) The citric acid structure proved complicated for SL. The molecule featured
3 carboxyl groups and a hydroxyl group so the majority answered that there were 4 acidic hydrogens
(b)(ii) Very few candidates showed a single COOH group ionizing to give COO- and so there were very few
scripts with the correct response
(b)(iii) Very few responses correctly identified citric acid as weak with a correct reason such as
the partial dissociation of a weak acid
(c) Almost all candidates could correctly calculate the pH as 2.6

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.2.SL.TZ1.2] May 2024 Paper 2 SL Q2
(a)(i) The calculation of q did not cause many problems- only very weak candidates added 273 to the
temperature difference or thought that propan-1-ol was heated rather than water.
(a)(ii) The calculation of % error of heat absorbed by the water was quite poorly done and needs to be
understood and practiced more.
(a)(iii) The vast number of candidates stated increasing the number of trials but very few then went on to
average the results and so lost the mark. Another alternative answer was to use a more precise
thermometer, but many incorrectly suggested a more accurate one instead.
(b)(i) The main error was that the Mr of propanol was not calculated, with a significant number of
candidates introducing bond energies for some reason. Those that did do a correct calculation often lost
the mark for not putting a - sign to indicate the reaction was exothermic.
(b)(ii) % error was generally calculated well,
(b)(iii) Heat loss was the most prevalent and correct response but many did not respond with how to
prevent it by using insulation.
(c) (i) Here the identification of organic class and functional group-alcohol/hydroxyl was quite well
answered but some had hydroxide as a response and others inverted the answers.
(c)(ii) Hydrogen bonding was the main answer here as the strongest IMF with dipole-dipole being
suggested quite often.
(c)(iii) London/Dispersion forces were the correct answer but again dipole-dipole and Hydrogen bonding
were incorrect popular answers

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.2.SL.TZ1.3] May 2024 Paper 2 SL Q3
(a) The equilibrium expression was well done
(b) Some candidates framed the response in terms of rate and so lost the mark for this question or stated
the equilibrium shifted right correctly without explaining it was because it was an endothermic reaction
(c)There was a disappointing response to this question as it has been seen many times. Few students
correctly annotated the Maxwell- Boltzmann graph and explained it well to gain 3 marks

(d) Identifying the activation energy of the catalyst linked to how well they answered part (c ), and as a
result the responses were disappointing.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.2.SL.TZ1.4] May 2024 Paper 2 SL Q4
(a)(i) Most candidates could get the correct oxidation numbers, however a few still lost marks for 2+ etc
instead of +2 or just 2
(a)(ii) Most candidates could correctly identify the reducing and oxidizing agents.
(b)(i) Most candidates had a correct Lewis structure for CO2, however some had single bonds between the
C and the O bonds. Many had bent molecules even when they had the correct double bonds around
carbon. We did not penalize this but it meant they went wrong later in the question.
(b)(ii) Most candidates put the correct dipole moments
(b)(iii) Many candidates had 1 mark for saying linear and non-polar, but few had 2 marks by explaining
there were only 2 electron domains and there was a symmetrical distribution of charge in the molecule.
b(iv) This should have been an easy question, so it was disappointing than so many candidates
answered that CO2 was a problem in terms of ozone depletion instead of climate change.
b(v) However, most candidates could state that CO was less stable than CO2 as it had higher enthalpy.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.2.SL.TZ1.5] May 2024 Paper 2 SL Q5
(a) The electron configuration was well done.
(b) Some students could suggest a property of sulfur that made it a nonmetal- however too many used
chemical properties or suggested it was a gas.
(c)As many candidates had no idea of the formulae for either of the oxides of sulfur they could not correctly
construct the simple equation required

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.2.SL.TZ1.6] May 2024 Paper 2 SL Q6
(a) Most could calculate the RAM correctly
(b)(i) The nickel ion was well done-although there were some errors.
(b)(ii) The majority of candidates had the correct formula for the nickel ion but a

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · recommendations] May 2024 Paper 3 HL
Candidates should be encouraged to use appropriate terminology, for instance, when to use hydroxy or
hydroxyl group instead of hydroxide, and distinguishing clearly between elements, atoms and nuclei.
Chemical terminologies should be taught carefully with enough practice and examples of application of
keywords for each topic.
Candidates should be encouraged to show working clearly for calculation-based questions, with the
correct number of significant figures and units. They should start with the formula or equation rather than
a jumbled array of numbers, and make it as easy as possible for an examiner to follow their working to
award ECF marks where applicable.
Where self-study is practiced for option topics, time should be taken by teachers to stress key points and
keywords required. Concepts that require understanding and application should be explicitly taught.

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · general] May 2024 Paper 3 SL
Over 5300 candidates sat this paper and, like last year, candidates found the paper very challenging with
the mean mark again being ~10/35 (29%). This was however quite skewed by the small number of higher
scoring candidates, so over 60% scored <10; the mode was 5 (14%). As commented last year, this is
noticeably different to May 2019, and the preceding years, when the mean was ~13 (37%), with a much
smaller proportion of candidates achieving a mark of 5 or under. It seems that students found Section A
particularly difficult, with the mean mark being <4/15 (25%). This is significantly lower than the equivalent
Section A mark in May 2019, when the mean was >6 (43%). Could this be an indication that current
candidates are carrying out fewer laboratory based investigations?
Sadly only 69 teachers took the time to complete the feedback form. About half of these felt the paper
difficult. It was however considered to be of appropriate level by ~80%, whilst the remainder thought it
was too difficult. The clarity of wording, presentation and readability of the paper were considered to be
of a good or very good standard by about 60% of teachers, whilst about 40% regarded them as acceptable
and a couple rated them poor. Teachers considered the papers good (~70%) or acceptable (~30%) for
suitability and inclusivity. Negative comments were mainly related to a lack of clarity about exactly what
was required for some of the questions in Section A, and these will be addressed in those questions.

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · recommendations] May 2024 Paper 3 SL
Train candidates to read the question carefully about:
• what exactly it is asking (including units or precision specified for the answer)
• the command term used and the implications of this
• how it relates to previous parts of the question (consider the whole picture)
• the number of marks available
Give students practice in writing clear explanations to support the answers they have given.
Ensure that are conversant with answers to questions frequently asked in the past, to avoid making similar
mistakes, particularly with regard
Encourage students to the use language precisely; examples include:
• Explicitly naming the type of intermolecular force being referred to rather than using the generic term
• Explain aqueous solubility as resulting from hydrogen bonding rather than polarity; many quite polar
molecules (e.g. CHCl3) are insoluble in water
• Discuss reaction rates in terms of frequency of collision rather than the probability or number of
collisions

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · recommendations] May 2024 Paper 2 HL
• Read the questions carefully before attempting to answer, do not rush to put pen to paper. Doing so
led to mistakes, for example in 3b(i) not reading sodium oxide and using a sulfur oxide in the chemical
equation; in 3 (c) ii, not reading that what had to be suggested was the composition of a buffer
with units" had to be provided.
• Go beyond learning a definition by heart. For example, when asked to define a bond, the first idea is
that it the result of an electrostatic attraction, so this cannot be omitted ever if the concept is
understood.
• Learn organic reaction mechanisms, understanding the importance of drawing curly arrows accurately
as they represent the specific movement of electrons.
• When writing equations for electron transfer at electrodes in electrolytical cells, understand that the
direction of the arrow indicates the product, thus "Na → Na+ + e- " is not showing that Na is produced at
the electrode but the contrary. This was a very common mistake.
• Topics/Concepts that should be considered carefully: knowledge/understanding of resonance,
bonding, use of units, significant figures vs decimal places (even if not examined).
• Stress the need to check units carefully.
Communication:
• Try to answer within the space provided or use extra sheets of paper, clearly indicating this in the
provided box.
• Draw diagrams with the correct type of pens provided.
• Try to ensure handwriting is legible.
• Comparing/contrasting requires references to both items that are being examined in these terms.

[EXAMINER REPORT 24M.2.SL.TZ2.1] May 2024 Paper 2 SL Q1
Over half of the candidates gave a correct answer by stating that the percentages of carbon and hydrogen
did not add up to 100% or that the compound contained oxygen. Some candidates simply stated that
hydrocarbons contain carbon and hydrogen only without relating it to the data provided in the question,
and hence did not score the mark. Other candidates stated that another element must be present but did
not use the information about the combustion products to deduce that it was oxygen. Weaker candidates
commented on an incorrect ratio of C:H or that hydrocarbons should contain oxygen showing a lack of
conceptual understanding.
A generally well answered question. The average mark was 1.35 out of 2 marks. The majority of candidates
calculated the amounts of carbon and hydrogen in a 100g sample gaining the first mark and many of them
went on to deduce the correct empirical formula. The most common mistake was not identifying that
oxygen was present in the compound.
This was a relatively challenging question that discriminated well between high scoring and low scoring
candidates. Over half of the candidates attempted a calculation of the molar mass using the data
provided, and many of them reached a correct value. Some candidates struggled with rearranging the
ideal gas and density equations, often giving up without obtaining a value for the M r. It was good to see

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · recommendations] May 2024 Paper 2 SL
Students should keep track of the information provided in the question to help them eliminate certain
alternatives during problem solving. A significant proportion of candidates did not make good use of the
information provided at the start of Question 1 this session. Moreover, please train students to reread the
question and ensure they are addressing precisely what is required.
It is important to provide plenty of opportunities for students to deduce Lewis structures, electron pair
and molecular geometries and bond angles for unfamiliar compounds. Students were not confident in
this area this session. Also to provide plenty of opportunities to identify the intermolecular forces based
on the structure and compare their strengths in different compounds, as students continued to show
weakness in this area.
Encourage students to write thorough explanations taking care to use the appropriate and accurate
ease in reaction rate.
Ensure students conduct plenty of investigations in the lab, and have opportunities to analyze data
including graphs and calculations. This will deepen their understanding and help them tackle new data in
unfamiliar situations.

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · general] May 2024 Paper 3 HL
We received detailed feedback from 326 schools this session. Most of the teachers (83%) found the paper
of appropriate difficulty although 17% described it as too difficult. When compared to the previous Paper
3, given in May 2023, 5% felt it was a little easier, 52% of the teachers felt it was of a similar standard, 31%
felt it was a little more difficult, and 12% felt it was much more difficult. In terms of inclusivity and suitability
the responses were very similar with approximately 75% reporting the paper as good to very good and
most of the other responses reporting the paper as acceptable. The readability of the paper received
similar comments with 64% describing the paper as good to excellent and 28% describing it as acceptable.
The presentation of the paper and clarity were also generally considered acceptable to very good by over
90% of the teacher responses. There were some concerns expressed for second language learners. The
paper was equitable for a diverse religious, ethnic, and gender population with no inclusivity issues.

they have a qualified need for extended time and potentially the use of molecular modelling kits when
molecular diagrams are too challenging to visually interpret.

every statement within the syllabus on each exam, but each sub-topic is represented in approximate
relative amounts based on the hours given to teach the content. Papers are also set to a strict markscheme
to provide for consistent marking between examiners.

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · recommendations] May 2024 Paper 3 HL
• The experimental laboratory programme should be integrated with the rest of the course and students
should be familiar with the application of lab techniques for all topics and the options taught. The use
of computational models should also be encouraged whenever possible.
• It is important to allocate sufficient class time to cover every part of the option in detail. It is critical that
core chemical principles are integrated in the option selected as it is taught.
• Candidates continue to struggle with questions that require explanations, interpretations, or multiple
steps. Very often they addressed only one part of the question while neglecting the others.
• The interpretation of command terms continues to be an issue. Students should be provided with a list
of the command terms and their definitions, so they are familiar with expectations for each individual
term and how they are applied in a variety of questions and responses. Students seem to especially
• Candidates should always look at the associated marks allocations in questions. Together with the
command terms the marks provide guidance on the depth expected by examiners for each answer.
• Provide training during the course in addressing questions and producing concise arguments.
Superfluous comments achieve no extra mark and may lead the student to lose focus.
• Candidates should not repeat the question in their response as no marks will be awarded for statements
from the stem of the question.
• Students do not have to answer questions in complete sentences. They may focus their responses as
bullet points.
• Converse arguments are accepted. For students writing their exams in a second language this may help
produce their arguments.
• Please encourage candidates to state their answers to calculations to a proper number of significant
figures and discourage rounding after each step or prior to reporting their final value. When they write
down a final value, encourage them to think about the correct sign based on the process.
•
Practice in the precise use of language and chemical terms throughout the course (e.g.,
atom/molecule/ion/particle) when writing answers to questions.

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · recommendations] May 2024 Paper 3 SL
As we transition to the 2025 curriculum, it's still valuable to include some comments that provide a
comprehensive view of the candidates' performance and can serve as a reference point for future
assessments.
• It is important to allocate sufficient class time to cover every part of the option material. It is critical that
core chemical principles are integrated in the option selected as it is taught.
• Candidates continue to struggle with questions that require explanations, interpretations, or multiple
steps. Very often they addressed only one part of the question while neglecting the others. Teachers
should provide practice in training students for producing concise arguments during classroom work
and assessments.
• Graphical analysis needed for experiments deserves greater attention.
• Candidates should realize that arguments repeating the stem do not receive any credit.
• Students should provide detailed work even if they found results using their calculators. The application
of Error Carried Forward can help them obtain more points when intermediate steps are wrong.
• Concepts related to Chemical Bonding and Intermolecular forces should be integrated with most topics.
• The interpretation and correct application of the command terms continues to be an issue. Students
should be directed to the command terms in the Subject Guide and their definitions. This should be
followed with ample opportunity to apply these terms during class work, classroom assessment and
then formal assessments.
• Candidates should always look at the associated marks allocated to a question. It should be explained
to the students that the marks allocated along with the command terms provide guidance for the depth
of the response required.
• Teachers should train students to be specific in their answers using correct subject specific terminology-
for example amount in chemistry refers to moles and molecules is not the same as particles.
• Candidates should write their answers within the space provided for each question (the box); examiners
cannot see answers written outside the space. Use extra sheet of papers to continue writing the answer
with the correct and complete question number identifying the answer.
• The handwriting continues to be an issue. Students should be reminded repeatedly during classwork

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · recommendations] May 2025 Paper 2 SL
Whenever possible, teachers should:
• Provide comments, partials, and an overall mark for each marking criterion. Holistic results of
individual criteria often disagree with the use of partials and the model of best fit.
• Refer to the Teacher Support Material (TSM) for detailed guidelines.
• When the material is borderline in two criteria, choosing the upper band in one and the lower in
the other is sometimes wise.
• Using grade descriptors can help determine if the overall mark has been too strict or generous.
• It’s very helpful if the work is annotated with the strands for each criterion, as shown in the TSM.
Schools should rigorously adopt the “best-fit” model and avoid awarding high bands when any
descriptor is unmet.
• Ensure that the work is anonymous. The candidate’s name, the school’s name, and the session
numbers must all be removed before scanning and uploading, both from the candidate and the
teacher’s mark sheet.
• Be careful when uploading the material. The work uploaded is the final one. Check that all the
pages are scanned, and that symbols, equations and data are clear.
• Images, graphs and tables should be of a reasonable size.
• Do not schedule the action stage of the individual investigation for the end of the teaching
program when there will not be sufficient time left to revise or repeat a method.
• Plan an experimental program that introduces and practices the skills the students need for the
IA.
• Introduce the command terms in the assessment criteria to students so they understand the
difference between state, describe, explain and justify.
• Show students some of the exemplary material and get them to use the assessment criteria.
• Get students to visualize/plan how to use the time provided for the practical part of the IA.
• Use the assessment criteria when providing feedback on other practical work.
• Teachers should approve only those investigations that allow students to satisfy the expectations
of the set criterion clearly.
• Both teachers and students should carefully evaluate the choice of topics to see if it allows enough
opportunity to carry out an in-depth investigation within the available time and resources.
• Topics beyond the curriculum can be encouraged with due support.
• Ensure that students are not repeating an experiment already carried out in the course.
• Ensure the investigation doesn’t stray from chemistry.

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · recommendations] May 2025 Paper 2 SL
• In the absence of the Personal Engagement criterion, students are increasingly selecting safe, well-
known topics. While this may ease the planning process, it limits critical thinking and originality.
Teachers should encourage students to formulate research questions that, even if based on
standard methodologies, reflect a personal angle or a specific variation that adds intellectual
depth and ownership.

• Students should be encouraged to remain within the 10-hour work period for the assessment.
More complex work with multiple independent variables rarely benefits students in terms of their
learning or grades. This often means they are more likely to make mistakes when processing large
quantities of data and have difficulty meeting the 3000-word limit.
• Discourage overambitious research questions that cannot be answered with the proposed
methodology and vague terms, e.g.’ extent’ and ‘efficient’.
• Including more than one research question and independent variable is rarely advisable except
for databased investigations.
• Check that suggested ranges are consistent with the presented context.
• Guide students in selecting independent variables that are genuinely manipulable and dependent
variables that can be measured with appropriate accuracy and precision.
• Independent variables should be quantified, and relationship study is highly recommended.
• Given the generally good performance in the Research Design criterion, students benefit from
having a clear structure. Teachers are encouraged to emphasize key components such as
theoretical background, safety, and procedural clarity. However, care should be taken not to
reduce the task to a template-driven exercise — students should be guided to understand why
each section is necessary, not just how to complete it.
• Provide structured support in planning without over-scaffolding.
• The background must be specific to the research question and the context of the investigation
and not journalistic in nature. It should include all relevant chemical equations.
• Students should be discouraged from writing copious background information that does not
specifically address their study’s context. Instead, they should focus on how current chemical

• Avoid relying on a method proposed in any given source and check its validity with other reliable

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · recommendations] May 2025 Paper 1B HL
• The experimental laboratory programme should be fully integrated with the rest of the course.
Students should be familiar with the application of the lab techniques listed in the guide and they
should be related to the topics taught. The use of computational models should also be
encouraged whenever possible.
a       International Baccalaureate
Baccalaureat International
Bachillerato Internacional
• Students should reflect on safety protocols, evaluate apparatus, and understand how
measurement uncertainties affect data accuracy.
• Targeted practice with graphing and data interpretation is strongly recommended. Students
should be taught how to draw curves of best fit and how to interpret or deduce mathematical
relationships between variables, such as absorbance and concentration. Integration with
mathematics lessons or interdisciplinary teaching may help reinforce these skills.
• Candidates continue to struggle with questions that require explanations, interpretations, or
multiple steps. Very often they addressed only one part of the question while neglecting the
others. Candidates should receive more exposure to structured, multi-part questions that require
interpretation, synthesis, and explanation. Many students currently address only a portion of such
questions.
• Encourage students to evaluate and justify their experimental decisions, such as choosing
equipment based on precision or suggesting method improvements. Practice tasks should include
identifying sources of error and explaining the impact on results.
• The interpretation of command terms continues to be an issue. Students should be provided with
a list of the command terms and their definitions, so they are familiar with expectations for each
individual term and how they are applied in a variety of questions and responses. Students seem
to especially struggle with “compare and contrast” statements which require BOTH items being
discussed to be mentioned for one mark and “explain” which typically requires more than one
concept for each mark.
• Candidates should always look at the associated marks allocations in questions. Together with the
command terms the marks provide guidance on the depth expected by examiners for each
answer.
• Provide training during the course in addressing questions and producing concise arguments.

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · recommendations] May 2025 Paper 1B HL
Superfluous comments achieve no extra mark and may lead the student to lose focus.
• Candidates should not repeat the question in their response as no marks will be awarded for
statements from the stem of the question.
• Students are not required to answer questions in complete sentences. They may focus their
responses as bullet points.
• Converse arguments are accepted. For students writing their exams in a second language this may
facilitate producing their arguments.
• Please encourage candidates to state their answers to calculations to an appropriate number of
significant figures and discourage rounding after each step or prior to reporting their final value.
They should use the values given including atomic masses as shown on the periodic table, not
rounded to whole numbers. When they write down a final value, encourage them to think about

synonyms of ‘groups,’ and to read questions carefully to ensure that they answer every part of the
question. Practice in the precise use of language and chemical terms throughout the course (e.g.,
atom/molecule/ion/particle) when writing answers to questions.

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · general] May 2025 Paper 2 SL
Paper 2 covered a broad and representative range of syllabus content, and overall the paper was
considered accessible and well-balanced by teachers. While a significant number of candidates were
able to engage effectively with recall-based questions, performance varied markedly on those
requiring application, interpretation of data, and multi-step calculations. Also, the widespread lack
of precision in definitions, diagram labelling, and chemical terminology hindered candidate success.

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · recommendations] May 2025 Paper 2 SL
Whenever possible, teachers should:
• Provide comments, partials, and an overall mark for each marking criterion. Holistic results of
individual criteria often disagree with the use of partials and the model of best fit.
• Refer to the Teacher Support Material (TSM) for detailed guidelines.
• When the material is borderline in two criteria, choosing the upper band in one and the lower in
the other is sometimes wise.
• Using grade descriptors can help determine if the overall mark has been too strict or generous.
• It’s very helpful if the work is annotated with the strands for each criterion, as shown in the TSM.
Schools should rigorously adopt the “best-fit” model and avoid awarding high bands when any
descriptor is unmet.
• Ensure that the work is anonymous. The candidate’s name, the school’s name, and the session
numbers must all be removed before scanning and uploading, both from the candidate and the
teacher’s mark sheet.
• Be careful when uploading the material. The work uploaded is the final one. Check that all the
pages are scanned, and that symbols, equations and data are clear.
• Images, graphs and tables should be of a reasonable size.
• Do not schedule the action stage of the individual investigation for the end of the teaching
programme when there will not be sufficient time left to revise or repeat a method.
• Plan an experimental programme that introduces and practices the skills the students need for
the IA.
• Introduce the command terms in the assessment criteria to students so they understand the
difference between state, describe, explain and justify.
• Show students some of the exemplary material and get them to use the assessment criteria.
• Get students to visualize/plan how to use the time provided for the practical part of the IA.
• Use the assessment criteria when providing feedback on other practical work.
• Teachers should approve only those investigations that allow students to satisfy the expectations
of the set criterion clearly.
• Both teachers and students should carefully evaluate the choice of topics to see if it allows enough
opportunity to carry out an in-depth investigation within the available time and resources.
• Topics beyond the curriculum can be encouraged with due support.
• Ensure that students are not repeating an experiment already carried out in the course.

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · recommendations] May 2025 Paper 2 SL
• Ensure the investigation doesn’t stray from chemistry.
• In the absence of the Personal Engagement criterion, students are increasingly selecting safe, well-
known topics. While this may ease the planning process, it limits critical thinking and originality.
Teachers should encourage students to formulate research questions that, even if based on
standard methodologies, reflect a personal angle or a specific variation that adds intellectual
depth and ownership.
• Students should be encouraged to remain within the 10-hour work period for the assessment.
More complex work with multiple independent variables rarely benefits students in terms of their

learning or grades. This often means they are more likely to make mistakes when processing large
quantities of data and have difficulty meeting the 3000-word limit.
• Discourage overambitious research questions that cannot be answered with the proposed
methodology and vague terms, e.g.’ extent’ and ‘efficient’.
• Including more than one research question and independent variable is rarely advisable except
for databased investigations.
• Check that suggested ranges are consistent with the presented context.
• Guide students in selecting independent variables that are genuinely manipulable and dependent
variables that can be measured with appropriate accuracy and precision.
• Independent variables should be quantified, and relationship study is highly recommended.
• Given the generally good performance in the Research Design criterion, students benefit from
having a clear structure. Teachers are encouraged to emphasize key components such as
theoretical background, safety, and procedural clarity. However, care should be taken not to
reduce the task to a template-driven exercise — students should be guided to understand why
each section is necessary, not just how to complete it.
• Provide structured support in planning without over-scaffolding.
• The background must be specific to the research question and the context of the investigation
and not journalistic in nature. It should include all relevant chemical equations.
• Students should be discouraged from writing copious background information that does not
specifically address their study’s context. Instead, they should focus on how current chemical

theory relates to their investigation, how their independent variable could affect the dependent
variable in their context and the theory and methodology required to study this.
• Avoid relying on a method proposed in any given source and check its validity with other reliable
sources.
• Students should ask themselves if the proposed method allows them to answer their research
questions before collecting data. It’s equally valid to change the procedure or the research
question, however, in the last case should also check if the presented background continues to
be relevant.
• Students should carefully consider efficient sampling. For example, measurements on just one
tablet can’t be considered representative.
• Students should be aware that incorrect storage of their samples may invalidate their data and
conclusion.
• Check that the collected data is adequate to answer the research question, and if not, modify the
latter in terms of the technique implemented and the data gathered.
• Check the methodology for any missing key variable that would invalidate the conclusions drawn.
• Students should check that their databases have sufficient data to perform a reasonable analysis
before fully engaging in their investigations.
• Foster the practice of having the students prepare at least three separate samples for each
independent variable and measure each instead of measuring the same solution three times when
manipulating the independent variables.

volumetric glassware.

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · recommendations] May 2025 Paper 1B HL
• Work on the importance of taking all the necessary time to read a question carefully and then
answer specifically what is requested.
• Students need to understand the various command terms fully, and teachers should take time to
review them (across all three objectives) with students throughout the two years of the
programme to ensure they understand how to answer questions.
• Students should always look at the associated mark allocations in the questions. Together with
the command terms, the marks provide guidance on the depth expected by examiners for each
answer.
• Students are not required to answer questions in complete sentences. They may focus their
responses on bullet points.
• Laboratory work must lie at the heart of the IB chemistry programme.
• Ideally, students should be exposed to comprehensive experimental experience in a laboratory
with suitable facilities. Where this is not the case, other resources, such as simulated experiments,
should be sourced.
• Time management should allocate enough time during the course to experimental skills, so
students not only perform the required experiments but also have time to analyze experimental
techniques in full depth and detail.
• Students should practice providing the correct names for different correlations.
• Drawing best-fit lines/curves with a focus on equal spacing of points.
• Students should use a ruler and an adequate pencil to draw lines on graphs.
• Students should be alert to the number of arguments/statements required by the question and
avoid providing more to avoid penalizations resulting from the List Principle.
• Ensure that students recognize that a dependent variable is a measured variable. Values that are
calculated are derived.
• Practice with the Tools of Chemistry to ensure familiarity with the techniques and processes
mentioned in that part of the syllabus.
• Students should practice how to explain processes using the correct terminology.
• Ensure students are familiar with various types of contexts for titration, including redox titrations.
• Practice interpreting all kinds of graphs more extensively.
• Review equipment names and lab procedures frequently throughout the course.
• Practice explaining specific sources of error that are consistent with the directionality of the error.
• Teachers should make the students aware that converse arguments are accepted. For students

• Students should correctly identify the section of a question they are answering when using extra
pages. For example, 1d wasn’t enough as there were five sections for 1d.

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · recommendations] May 2025 Paper 1A SL
• Emphasise the difference between physical and chemical properties, and how this relates to the
properties of different isotopes of an element.
• Encourage students to draw Lewis formulas when determining the polarity of a molecule.
• Reinforce the interpretation of condensed structural formulas and encourage students to draw
displayed or skeletal formulas when tackling questions that involve a large variety of condensed
structural formulas.
• Give students a variety of chromatograms for them to learn which measurements are needed for
Rf calculations.
• Give students several opportunities to do IB and IB-style multiple-choice questions under exam
conditions. When reviewing the answers, prompt them to consider not only why the correct
answer is right, but also why the incorrect answers are wrong.
• Remind students to check the guidance given beneath each numbered “understanding” in the
guide. For example, the difference between acid and base strength and concentration in Reactivity
3.1.6.
• Remind students not to leave multiple-choice answers blank.

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · general] May 2025 Paper 1B SL
The introduction of Paper 1B brings a significant change to the external assessment model. It
primarily assesses the “Skills in the study of chemistry”. Compared to the 2016 curriculum’s
prescribed practical’s, students are now required to apply their practical knowledge more flexibly
and across a variety of different, unfamiliar contexts. Doing so often necessitates wordier questions
as the context of the question needs to be more extensively laid out.
Several teachers felt that the paper aligned well with the syllabus and placed greater emphasis on
practical skills compared to the legacy curriculum’s Paper 3 Section A. The feedback received on this
paper was very helpful and covered a variety of aspects including timing, question wording,
feedback on specific questions, use of command terms and overall impressions. Over 100 teachers
provided feedback on SL Paper 1B in this time zone. Thank you.
Over 90 % of teachers rated the difficulty level as appropriate, and just under 10 % felt it was too
difficult. Around 35 % of respondents found the paper to be a little or much more difficult than last
year. The mean mark achieved on this paper was 8.52 out of 25 possible marks.
In terms of inclusivity and suitability of the paper, around 80% of teachers considered it to be “good”
or “very good”, with the remaining responses rating it as acceptable. The comments described positive
reactions to the readability of the paper, with most questions perceived as clear and not excessively wordy.
The readability, presentation, and clarity of the paper were described as “good” or “very good” by
just over 80 % of teachers. A handful (2 %) indicated concerns in these areas. In the comments
concerns were raised relating to the presentation of the combined paper sections 1A and 1B as
students need to manage their time well as well as the various papers and resources on their desks.

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · general] May 2025 Paper 2 HL
This paper was of appropriate level by 90% of the 158 schools that responded to the G2 report,
among whom almost 60% considered it to be of similar difficulty to M24 and 25% found it a little
more or much more difficult. Other issues referred to qualities of the paper such as inclusivity,
suitability, readability, presentation and clarity were good or very good by 80% of schools. Being the
first session with the new syllabus that has introduced a significantly different approach, it was
interesting to find that teachers found that the exam reflected the more interwoven concepts of the
course through the themes of structure and reactivity for example. Many teachers considered it to
be a nice balance between familiar and unfamiliar contexts. While many teachers felt that there were
many calculations, which some students might have struggled with, they also felt that there were no
surprises—everything was within the core of the Chemistry syllabus.
One of the aspects to be noted is that the percentage of questions attempted was higher than in
previous sessions and even very weak students were able to provide reasonable answers to the few
questions they were able to answer. The questions that were answered incorrectly or left unanswered
were often common to very good students so it could be expected that they were either
misunderstood or too challenging. It is also possible that while they were topics that they were
familiar with, the combination of different aspects of chemistry of a compound or element which is
the basis of the new curricular approach is still not fully embraced by students and teachers alike.
A recurring comment from teachers referred to the fact that the language used in the paper was
concise and free of unnecessary complexity. Key instructions and questions were presented clearly,
aiding understanding for students who additional language learners are.

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · recommendations] May 2025 Paper 2 HL
• Firstly, some very practical points to avoid losing easy marks:
• Ions must be written as Xn+/- and oxidation states as X+/- n
• Rate always includes the mention of time.
• Check units: this is the most common mistake in calculations involving entropy, enthalpy and ∆G.
• Be aware of connectivity of atoms when drawing organic structures, such as in question 1di
(acetonitrile).
• Unit conversions/decimal places: train students to read questions carefully in terms of command
terms, units, and precision
• Pay attention to the change in requirements for answering the same type of questions. For
example, "complementary colour of light absorbed" is no longer a point to get the mark.
• Pay attention to the requirements for significant figures.
• Encourage students to show all the calculations. Rounding must be done at the end.
• Practice in sketching and labelling graphs.
• Teach students to indicate the question clearly in the extra paper. It is quite common for an
examiner to have to be following incorrectly numbered answers in extra pages.
• Keep answers concise: there seemed to be a significant increase in the number of students using
the answer booklet to complete questions, however the style of the questions has not changed
significantly from past exams.
a       International Baccalaureate
Baccalaureat International
Bachillerato Internacional
• Students should always look at the number of marks in the question. In combination with
command terms it would help students to provide an answer in a reasonable depth.
• Develop Multi-Step Problem-Solving Skills: many errors stemmed from difficulties in handling
multi-stage calculations (e.g., Q3a vi and Q4b). Teachers should incorporate more complex
problems that require integrating different areas of the syllabus—such as equilibrium,
thermodynamics, and stoichiometry—into regular practice as this will be norm with the approach
chosen in the new curricular design.
• Improve Data Interpretation and Analytical Skills: questions involving the interpretation of graphs,
spectra, or structural features (e.g., electrolysis products) should be practiced more frequently.

a (i) A reasonable number of students had a correct Lewis formula for HCN; however, some had a

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · recommendations] May 2025 Paper 2 SL
• Teachers are strongly advised to refer to past examination papers and the corresponding mark
schemes to assist students with examination preparation.
• Students should read questions carefully to avoid missing parts of the question. This ensures that
they answer appropriately, precisely, and use correct terminology.
• Too often, students are not giving reasons for their answers, even though it is explicitly asked for
in the question.
• For example, Q2a(iii): Explain why, in terms of nuclear charge and the shielding of the valence
electrons, the first ionization energy of thallium is lower than that of lead, but a significant number
of students are still missing out on the nuclear charge and shielding in their answers. The students
are still writing “there are more collisions between molecules” without referring to time when
explaining the increase in reaction rate.
• Teachers should encourage students to note the number of marks allocated to a question and
correlate this to their response to ensure it is sufficiently detailed. This will enable students to
avoid just writing rambling statements, hoping that they will pick up marks somewhere in their
answer.
• Students must know the meaning of the different command terms that appear in the assessment
statements and the examination papers.
• Teachers should emphasise the importance of clearly set out calculations. Significant figures
should be considered in all calculation-type questions. Students should read questions carefully
to avoid errors in units.
• Students must be instructed to use the chemistry data booklet during the chemistry course so
that they are familiar with the data booklet.
• Some students are writing more than one answer, hoping the examiners will pick up the correct
answer. This is not encouraged because a correct response followed by an incorrect response
nullifies the mark of that question.
Students should write legibly so examiners can read responses.

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · recommendations] May 2025 Paper 2 SL
Whenever possible, teachers should:
• Provide comments, partials, and an overall mark for each marking criterion. Holistic results of
individual criteria often disagree with the use of partials and the model of best fit.
• Refer to the Teacher Support Material (TSM) for detailed guidelines.
• When the material is borderline in two criteria, choosing the upper band in one and the lower in
the other is sometimes wise.
• Using grade descriptors can help determine if the overall mark has been too strict or generous.
• It’s very helpful if the work is annotated with the strands for each criterion, as shown in the TSM.
Schools should rigorously adopt the “best-fit” model and avoid awarding high bands when any
descriptor is unmet.
• Ensure that the work is anonymous. The candidate’s name, the school’s name, and the session
numbers must all be removed before scanning and uploading, both from the candidate and the
teacher’s mark sheet.
• Be careful when uploading the material. The work uploaded is the final one. Check that all the
pages are scanned, and that symbols, equations and data are clear.
• Images, graphs and tables should be of a reasonable size.
• Do not schedule the action stage of the individual investigation for the end of the teaching
programme when there will not be sufficient time left to revise or repeat a method.
• Plan an experimental programme that introduces and practices the skills the students need for
the IA.
• Introduce the command terms in the assessment criteria to students so they understand the
difference between state, describe, explain and justify.
• Show students some of the exemplary material and get them to use the assessment criteria.
• Get students to visualize/plan how to use the time provided for the practical part of the IA.
• Use the assessment criteria when providing feedback on other practical work.
• Teachers should approve only those investigations that allow students to satisfy the expectations
of the set criterion clearly.
• Both teachers and students should carefully evaluate the choice of topics to see if it allows enough
opportunity to carry out an in-depth investigation within the available time and resources.
• Topics beyond the curriculum can be encouraged with due support.
• Ensure that students are not repeating an experiment already carried out in the course.

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · recommendations] May 2025 Paper 2 SL
• Ensure the investigation doesn’t stray from chemistry.
• In the absence of the Personal Engagement criterion, students are increasingly selecting safe, well-
known topics. While this may ease the planning process, it limits critical thinking and originality.
Teachers should encourage students to formulate research questions that, even if based on
standard methodologies, reflect a personal angle or a specific variation that adds intellectual
depth and ownership.
• Students should be encouraged to remain within the 10-hour work period for the assessment.
More complex work with multiple independent variables rarely benefits students in terms of their

learning or grades. This often means they are more likely to make mistakes when processing large
quantities of data and have difficulty meeting the 3000-word limit.
• Discourage overambitious research questions that cannot be answered with the proposed
methodology and vague terms, e.g.’ extent’ and ‘efficient’.
• Including more than one research question and independent variable is rarely advisable except
for databased investigations.
• Check that suggested ranges are consistent with the presented context.
• Guide students in selecting independent variables that are genuinely manipulable and dependent
variables that can be measured with appropriate accuracy and precision.
• Independent variables should be quantified, and relationship study is highly recommended.
• Given the generally good performance in the Research Design criterion, students benefit from
having a clear structure. Teachers are encouraged to emphasize key components such as
theoretical background, safety, and procedural clarity. However, care should be taken not to
reduce the task to a template-driven exercise — students should be guided to understand why
each section is necessary, not just how to complete it.
• Provide structured support in planning without over-scaffolding.
• The background must be specific to the research question and the context of the investigation
and not journalistic in nature. It should include all relevant chemical equations.
• Students should be discouraged from writing copious background information that does not
specifically address their study’s context. Instead, they should focus on how current chemical

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · recommendations] May 2025 Paper 2 SL
theory relates to their investigation, how their independent variable could affect the dependent
variable in their context and the theory and methodology required to study this.
• Avoid relying on a method proposed in any given source and check its validity with other reliable
sources.
• Students should ask themselves if the proposed method allows them to answer their research
questions before collecting data. It’s equally valid to change the procedure or the research
question, however, in the last case should also check if the presented background continues to
be relevant.
• Students should carefully consider efficient sampling. For example, measurements on just one
tablet can’t be considered representative.
• Students should be aware that incorrect storage of their samples may invalidate their data and
conclusion.
• Check that the collected data is adequate to answer the research question, and if not, modify the
latter in terms of the technique implemented and the data gathered.
• Check the methodology for any missing key variable that would invalidate the conclusions drawn.
• Students should check that their databases have sufficient data to perform a reasonable analysis
before fully engaging in their investigations.
• Foster the practice of having the students prepare at least three separate samples for each
independent variable and measure each instead of measuring the same solution three times when
manipulating the independent variables.
• Students should master the correct procedure of making standard solutions and dilutions using
volumetric glassware.

• Discourage the use of pictograms that add minimum value.
• Encourage procedures to use lower quantities of chemicals to preserve the environment and
check that your favorite source for risk assessment and disposal takes biomagnification and
bioaccumulation into account.
• If practical work is possible, encourage students to process and reflect on data while collecting it
so they can immediately adapt or extend their procedural phase if the data are proving insufficient
or erroneous. Also, processing data while it is being collected is always good practice.
• More emphasis is needed on the quality of data, and its dispersion can be seen as an opportunity

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · recommendations] May 2025 Paper 2 SL
to understand its impact and explore ways to deal with it. It is important not to just calculate it
but then ignore it.
• Please verify that your students have collected the data they report.
• Provide targeted practice on graph analysis, trend identification, and using uncertainty and
statistical tools. Teach students to critically evaluate their data rather than simply presenting raw
results.
• The tools described in T3- Processing uncertainties and Graphing should be introduced early in
the course and integrated into as many labs as possible.
• Dedicate time to teaching proper data presentation, particularly for tables.
• Discourage your students from implementing statistical analysis they don’t understand or lack the
time to collect sufficient data.
• Double-check all calculations to identify any errors that might impact the reliability of the
conclusions.
• When performing sample calculations, students should be encouraged to clearly state which
experiment/trial they are based on.
• Students should try alternate best-fit lines before deciding on the final line that fits the data
plotted.
• Discourage your students from eliminating outliers simply because their results or trendlines don’t
match their original expectations.
• Teachers should emphasize that conclusions are not just results summaries but must include a
meaningful connection to chemical principles.
• Instruct students on how to effectively integrate secondary evidence or relevant chemical theory
to support and contextualize their conclusions. This will elevate their understanding and
argumentation beyond mere experimental results, addressing the observed weakness of
insufficient theoretical backing.
• Providing examples that model strong theoretical reasoning could help bridge this gap.
• Teach students that effective evaluations must go beyond listing weaknesses or limitations—they
should provide specific evidence from their investigation and assess each limitation’s impact on
the results’ reliability and validity. A more in-depth analysis could be fostered using checklists and
encouraging phrases such as “this may have led to…” or “this could have significantly affected…”
to show clear analytical reasoning. Teachers should gradually work with students to build these
skills by analyzing sample investigations, discussing the strengths and weaknesses of hypothetical

• Train students to evaluate their investigation specifically in terms of its reliability, reproducibility,
accuracy, and precision. Their suggested improvements should directly address how these aspects
of data quality could be enhanced. For instance, an improvement should explain how it would
lead to more precise measurements or more reliable data rather than just starting a change.
• Avoid “do more trials” or anything that was a fault of the design in Ev.
• Encourage the use of reliable resources.
• Rather than treating evaluation as a final task, please encourage students to reflect critically on
their design choices, challenges encountered during experimentation, and the quality of their data
in the labs forming the Experimental Programme and every stage of the individual investigation.
• Embed evaluative thinking early and often during the Experimental programme to foster a more
authentic understanding of the scientific process.

effectively, particularly when writing conclusions and addressing research questions. By
addressing these areas, future students will be better equipped to produce high-quality,

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · recommendations] May 2025 Paper 1A HL
It is difficult to generalise about multiple choice errors, but many seem to arise from students
misreading the question, indicating the need to pay more attention to what is being asked.
The low marks on the last half dozen questions might indicate that students were running out of
time. Students should therefore regularly practice taking multiple choice tests in order to develop
their technique, particularly with regard to leaving questions they are having difficulty with until the
end, in order that they know how much time is available to spend on them. They do however need
to clearly mark such questions so that they always enter an answer to every question, even if it’s only
a guess!

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · general] May 2025 Paper 1B HL
This was the first ever sitting of a Paper 1b and the impression was that the nature of the paper
came as something of a shock to many students. There were a number of questions when the
answers given by a large number of students gave the impression they had not even managed to

[EXAMINER OVERVIEW · recommendations] May 2025 Paper 1B SL
The development of students’ laboratory skills should be intentionally integrated into lesson
planning with a strong emphasis on inquiry-based learning. Students should be able to follow
written instructions to correctly perform experiments. They should be able to name the equipment
they use and understand the need for selecting apparatus based on precision requirements.
Students should understand the purpose and reasoning for the experimental steps undertaken, and
should reflect on experimental outcomes and limitations. Students should have specific training in
processing uncertainties and rounding values to the correct number of significant figures.
Although it can be effective to explain concepts with common language, it is important for teachers
to ensure that students use correct scientific language and chemistry terminology.
Teachers should instruct students on the correct way to label answers on additional sheets to enable
examiners to link these responses to those in the answer book.

candidate results showed a significant decrease in the numbers of students scoring below 30 marks
on the paper which was very pleasing.

equations were usually balanced and charges were shown on ions. Explanations were often detailed

skill.
